title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
description: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health minist
body: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

schema.headline: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway

title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
description: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early tra
body: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs. But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry. Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off."It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

schema.headline: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify

title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
description: Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge i
body: Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge."For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external. "Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge."The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said."Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal."If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

schema.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering

title: Pete Edochie: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor dies aged 79
description: Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.Known for his dee
body: Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes."As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said. Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers."Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

schema.headline: Pete Edochie: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor dies aged 79

title: Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been charged  by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles with possessing child sex abuse images
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been charged  by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles with possessing child sex abuse images.Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

schema.headline: Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images

title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
description: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports
body: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%. The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer."The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note."The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

schema.headline: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China

title: Canadian astronaut welcomes baby girl from space station
description: A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.Joshua Kutr
body: A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday."Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency. Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station. The couple have two older children, aged five and seven. "We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true. "We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017. Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space. The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing"."I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said. "It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

schema.headline: Canadian astronaut welcomes baby girl from space station

title: Taiwan election: Is China behind a wave of AI fakes and disinformation?
description: Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local
body: Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process."The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said."Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

schema.headline: Taiwan election: Is China behind a wave of AI fakes and disinformation?

title: US Army says controlled lead azide explosives blast in Iowa was 'huge success'
description: Figure caption, Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation siteByAna FaguyUpdated 4 hours agoThe US military has hailed as a "hu
body: Figure caption, Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation siteByAna FaguyUpdated 4 hours agoThe US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".President Donald Trump said reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations". Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising. "The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media."We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.Image source, Sandy MabeusMiddletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site. "We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down. The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened."We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened."The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday."I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"But there is also caution from some. Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds. But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

schema.headline: US Army says controlled lead azide explosives blast in Iowa was 'huge success'

title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC Russ
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC RussianUpdated 12:21 GMTAt least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.How we came to a figure near half a millionThe Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesIn most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

schema.headline: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war

title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
description: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, Preside
body: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap."I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet? Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter."Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology. State governments could also launch their own investigations.Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself."I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X."Congress has much to investigate," he said.While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed. Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large. In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption."Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year. The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules."It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday. "Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy. He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic). And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters. He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%. Last Friday alone, it fell 14%. US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed. And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

schema.headline: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks

title: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
description: Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sán
body: Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments."What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the  administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei."If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said Sánchez.He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image.Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left.Yet in Spain, Sánchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal.In a bullring in Valencia, the same day that Sánchez was staging his rally, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo told supporters that the last few years of Socialist-led government had been "insulting and even humiliating for a lot of people". He added: "We know them, they are capable of anything."A couple of days earlier, Ignacio Garriga, spokesman for Vox, had gone further, describing Sánchez as "a very dangerous psychopath".Both the PP and Vox have cast doubt on the neutrality of postal votes and votes cast by Spaniards abroad ahead of the election, suggesting that government manipulation could sway them in its favour."This is a campaign that is overwhelmingly ideological," said Cristina Monge, a political scientist at the Complutense University. "That means that it is not so much about voters rewarding or punishing a government's performance or the proposals being made, but about belonging to one or other ideological bloc."Much of the hostility to Sánchez stems from his reliance on hard-left and separatist parties.Ahead of the 2023 general election, he faced fierce criticism from the right for his reliance on the pro-independence EH Bildu coalition, which had links to the defunct Basque armed group ETA. After that vote, he was able to form a new administration with the support of another separatist party, Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for an amnesty for all Catalans facing legal action for their role in a failed 2017 bid for independence.At the time, Núñez Feijóo accused Sánchez of being "a prime minister who has bought his investiture in exchange for the judicial impunity of his partners".Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University, said those parliamentary partnerships "fed the rhetoric of the right and far right, which was that Pedro Sánchez is an amoral person without scruples – someone whose word can't be trusted and who just wants to remain in power".This legislation has been one of turmoil for Sánchez, during which he has been unable to push a single budget through parliament.In addition, the prime minister has been corralled by a litany of judicial investigations. He has acknowledged errors of judgement in trusting two close former associates in the Socialist Party, José Luis Ábalos, who has been given a 24-year-jail sentence for corruption-related crimes, and Santos Cerdán, who is due to go on trial on similar charges.By contrast, he has defended his former attorney general, Álvaro García Ortiz, who was barred from public office for revealing confidential information, and his brother, David, who was barred from office for nine years after being found guilty of irregularities in taking on a post as a regional arts director. In the most controversial case, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial for influence peddling. She denies wrongdoing and Sánchez has said the cases involving García Ortiz, his brother and wife are "nasty politics, not corruption", blaming them on efforts by his political opponents to use the judiciary to destabilise his government.Politicians on the right draw no such distinction between the various cases, and Vox leader Santiago Abascal describes the government as "a criminal mafia".María Pérez, a young office worker who has no political allegiance, says she is going to vote for the PP, partly because of her concerns about the country's housing crisis and the rail system, which has seen two major tragedies this year, but above all due to the judicial investigations."I think that Sánchez has lost credibility with all the corruption cases," she says. "It seems that everyone in government is involved… so I'm not sure I want them to continue governing. I believe it's time for a change."Allegations that Sánchez has co-opted state institutions, such as the CIS national research centre, which publishes opinion polls, and national broadcaster RTVE, have only compounded the right's view of him as a populist who has scant regard for the rule of law.However, with the far right seemingly set to enter government for the first time in Spain's democratic era, claims of demagoguery cut both ways.Politicians on the left say that coalition administrations formed by the PP and Vox in four of Spain's 17 regions are a blueprint for socially regressive policies they plan to implement on a national level after the election.In all four of those regions, Vox has negotiated the introduction of "national priority", which seeks to give Spaniards priority access to public services and subsidies ahead of foreigners.The Castilla y León region has also seen culture-related controversies driven by Vox. Most recently, a play about left-wing poet and dramatist Federico García Lorca, who was killed by right-wing rebels during the 1936-39 civil war, was cancelled in the region's capital, Valladolid, apparently at the behest of the Vox-controlled local culture ministry.Last month the same department published new guidelines governing the awarding of subsidies for films, stating that projects involving what it called "ideological indoctrination" would not be eligible. Spain's culture minister, Ernest Urtasun, described this as "an intolerable attempt at censorship".Susana Fuertes, a schoolteacher who will vote for the left on Sunday, said such moves are a sinister throwback to the dictatorship of Francisco Franco."These political messages take us back to the Franco era by talking about getting rid of basic civil rights regarding women, gender equality and immigration," she said. "All of this has been said in such an aggressive tone, with insults and lack of respect for people who don't share the same ideas."

schema.headline: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election

title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours
description: De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to
body: De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused. Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women. But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre. Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked."We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied. "We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives. He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.  Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers. Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded. The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces. A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage. Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.

schema.headline: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours

title: Phala Phala farm theft: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
description: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large su
body: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make"."It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report."[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane said.The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier. Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings. He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him. It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.Legal expert Professor Richard Calland told the BBC he had expected the court ruling, given what he termed as "fault lines" in the independent panel's report. Calland said the court's findings now meant that the impeachment process was "dead in the water [and] cannot continue".He said that any political party that wanted to revive it "would have to come up with a whole new basis" for this.Calland said political parties who want to hold Ramaphosa accountable would likely seek to appeal the ruling but it was unlikely parliament would also do so."So, the president's political career is now free of the cloud of impeachment," he said.

schema.headline: Phala Phala farm theft: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat

title: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
description: Image source, KCNA via Getty ImagesImage caption, Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a new reportB
body: Image source, KCNA via Getty ImagesImage caption, Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a new reportByJake KwonSeoul correspondent Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report, external documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty."The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself,  he adds.Image source, Courtesy Kim Bo-binImage caption, Kim Bo-bin has been living in South Korea for 15 years nowFirst established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An image from 2010 showing the inside of a state-sanctioned church in Pyongyang This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, North Koreans pay tribute to statues of the late Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong IlKim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A view of the city of Chongjin in North Korea's North Hamgyong provinceKim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them. In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?"Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps.Lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, says she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory.Image source, BBC/ Hosu LeeImage caption, Lee Young-joo first met a Christian after she escaped from North Korea into China   She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC.Kim says she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God."Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later.Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied.Today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told.Kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

schema.headline: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
